lesson.title: One Population, Two Questions
lesson.summary: A test for independence checks whether two categorical variables measured on the same single sample are associated in the population, using the same chi-square arithmetic as homogeneity but a genuinely different sampling structure.
lesson.body:
A test for independence asks a fundamentally different question than a test for homogeneity, even though, as you will see, the arithmetic underneath is identical. Independence starts with a single population and a single random sample from it, then records two categorical variables on every individual in that one sample, rather than one variable measured across several separately sampled groups. The question is whether those two variables are associated with each other in the population: does knowing an individual's value on one variable give you any information about their likely value on the other?

Here is a full worked example. A single random sample of 200 adults is surveyed, and each person is classified on two variables: how often they exercise, regular, occasional, or rarely, and how they would rate their sleep quality, good or poor. The results:

Good sleep: Regular 40, Occasional 35, Rarely 15, row total 90
Poor sleep: Regular 20, Occasional 40, Rarely 50, row total 110
Column totals: Regular 60, Occasional 75, Rarely 65. Grand total 200.

The null hypothesis of independence says exercise frequency and sleep quality have nothing to do with each other in this population, which is exactly what the expected counts assume: if the two variables really were independent, each cell's expected count would be row total times column total, divided by grand total, the same formula used for homogeneity, because independent and same distribution across groups turn out to be two descriptions of the identical no-relationship condition, just applied to different sampling designs. Working through each cell:

Good sleep, Regular: 90 times 60, divided by 200, equals 27
Good sleep, Occasional: 90 times 75, divided by 200, equals 33.75
Good sleep, Rarely: 90 times 65, divided by 200, equals 29.25
Poor sleep, Regular: 110 times 60, divided by 200, equals 33
Poor sleep, Occasional: 110 times 75, divided by 200, equals 41.25
Poor sleep, Rarely: 110 times 65, divided by 200, equals 35.75

All six expected counts are well above 5, the smallest is 27, so the large counts condition is satisfied easily. Now compute the chi-square contribution of each cell:

Good sleep, Regular: 40 minus 27, squared, divided by 27, equals 6.259
Good sleep, Occasional: 35 minus 33.75, squared, divided by 33.75, equals 0.046
Good sleep, Rarely: 15 minus 29.25, squared, divided by 29.25, equals 6.942
Poor sleep, Regular: 20 minus 33, squared, divided by 33, equals 5.121
Poor sleep, Occasional: 40 minus 41.25, squared, divided by 41.25, equals 0.038
Poor sleep, Rarely: 50 minus 35.75, squared, divided by 35.75, equals 5.680

Summing all six terms gives X squared is approximately 24.09. Degrees of freedom for a two-way table equal rows minus 1 times columns minus 1, here 2 minus 1 times 3 minus 1 equals 2. Chi-square distributions with exactly 2 degrees of freedom have a convenient exact formula for the area to the right of any value x, namely e raised to the power of negative x over 2. Plugging in 24.09 gives a P-value on the order of 0.000006, essentially zero. That is a dramatically small P-value, far below any conventional alpha level, pointing toward strong evidence of a real association between exercise frequency and sleep quality among the adults sampled, and the full conclusion writing process comes in a later chapter.

One caution worth flagging immediately: this was an observational survey, not a randomized experiment, so even overwhelming statistical evidence of association does not by itself establish that exercising more causes better sleep. It could, but confounding variables such as overall health, work schedule, or stress could also be driving both exercise habits and sleep quality at once.
